title: A Longitudinal Measurement of Privacy Policy Evolution for Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how privacy policies for mainstream large language model (LLM) providers evolve over time, with a focus on what kinds of data practices are disclosed and how those disclosures respond to product launches and regulatory pressure. The authors argue that LLM privacy policies are underexplored despite the sensitive and extensive personal data collected through prompts, uploads, feedback, and agentic tool use.

The study uses a longitudinal document-analysis approach rather than a participant-based intervention. The authors curate 74 historical privacy-policy versions and 115 supplemental privacy documents from 11 LLM providers across 5 countries, then extract and code 3,463 sentence-level edits between consecutive policy versions. They also compare these policies with older general-software privacy policies and propose a new taxonomy tailored to LLM-specific data practices.

The paper finds that LLM privacy policies are substantially longer, more complex, and more vague than traditional software policies. They increasingly disclose first-party collection of chat transcripts, AI outputs, and feedback; third-party interactions via plugins and downstream apps; model-training uses of user data; and more explicit rights and controls. The longitudinal analysis suggests that policy changes are often driven by product releases and, with some delay, by regulatory actions such as GDPR-related enforcement. The overall conclusion is that LLM privacy policies are evolving quickly but remain difficult to read, fragmented across supplemental documents, and still highly ambiguous.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Large language model services and chatbots used for general-purpose conversational and agentic interaction, with associated data collection and privacy-policy disclosures.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies privacy policies and policy evolution of mainstream LLM providers and their LLM services, including general references to chatbots and agentic systems, rather than evaluating a classroom-specific AI tool.

findings.finding_summary: In a longitudinal empirical study of 11 mainstream LLM providers, the authors collected 74 historical privacy policies and 115 supplemental documents and extracted 3,463 sentence-level edits. They found that LLM privacy policies are substantially longer than traditional software policies, require upper-college to graduate-level reading ability (median FKGL 14.77 in 2023, 15.66 in 2024, 15.74 in 2025), remain highly vague, and often expand disclosures about model training, third-party integrations, and user rights over time.
findings.measure: Privacy policy length, readability (Flesch-Kincaid grade level), vagueness, and longitudinal policy edits across LLM providers
findings.effect_size: Policies were around 53.6% longer than the 2019 general-software baseline
findings.sample_size: n=11 providers; 74 historical policies; 115 supplemental documents

quality_tier_rationale: This is a longitudinal empirical document-analysis study, but it does not evaluate instructional outcomes or classroom use. The evidence is observational and descriptive rather than experimental.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows meaningful policy evolution and privacy burden in LLM services, but it does not demonstrate direct educational impact or harm in K–12 instructional coaching or lesson feedback.
